summary: Teaches the causal explanation of Moon phases for ages 7-9: the Moon orbits Earth about once a month, makes no light of its own but reflects sunlight (so one half is always lit by the Sun), and the phases we see are caused by how much of that lit half faces us from Earth as the Moon moves around us. The central, hard idea is that phases are a viewing-angle effect, NOT the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon (that rarer event is a lunar eclipse). The canonical activity is a lit ball (Moon) orbiting the child's head (Earth) under a single lamp (Sun) so the child watches the lit fraction change from their own vantage point; screen models and a reference diagram support and extend this.
misconceptions: Believing phases are caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon (the single most common and persistent error) — rather than by our changing view of the lit half.
Thinking the Moon produces its own light, rather than reflecting the Sun's.
Believing clouds, or an object passing in front, cover the Moon to make the phases.
Thinking only part of the Moon is lit at any time (not realising a full hemisphere is always lit; what changes is our viewing angle).
Confusing the ordinary monthly phase cycle with a lunar eclipse (which IS Earth's shadow, but rare) — merging two different phenomena.
Assuming the Moon is only visible at night, or that a new moon means the Moon has 'gone away'.

activities.title: Ball-and-lamp: orbit the Moon around your own head
steps: In a darkened room, shine a single lamp (the Sun) on a ball (the Moon); notice one half of the ball is always bright and the other half dark.
Hold the ball at arm's length and slightly above head height (so your own shadow does not fall on it), stand with your head as Earth, and slowly turn all the way around so the ball orbits your head.

As you turn, watch how much of the bright half you can see and name the views you pass through: all of it (full), half the disc lit (quarter), a thin sliver (crescent), or none at all (new) — these appear at different points as you rotate, not only at the quarter-turns.
Say aloud for one position: 'The Moon is still fully half-lit by the lamp — I am just seeing more / less of the bright side from here.'
Point to where the dark side is pointing when you see a crescent, to confirm nothing is covering the Moon.
activities.insight: Phases are caused by our changing view of the always-half-lit Moon as it orbits, not by anything covering or shadowing it.

activities.title: Does the Moon make its own light?
steps: Put the ball where you can see its bright and dark halves.
Predict what happens to the ball if the lamp is switched off.
Switch off the lamp and observe: the ball goes dark, or only stays dimly visible from any other light leaking into the room, because it makes no light of its own.
Explain in a sentence where the Moon's glow comes from, using the word 'reflect'.
activities.insight: The Moon produces no light of its own; it shines only by reflecting the Sun's light, so with no Sun there is nothing to see.

activities.title: Where is Earth's shadow really? Separating phases from eclipses
steps: For an ordinary crescent or half phase, work out where the Sun is, where the Moon is, and where Earth's shadow would stretch (straight away from the Sun).
Check whether Earth's shadow actually falls on the Moon in that position — in ordinary phases it points off into empty space, nowhere near the Moon.
Describe the special, rare line-up when Earth is EXACTLY in line between the Sun and the full Moon, so the shadow does reach the Moon — name this a lunar eclipse.
Write one sentence stating what causes ordinary phases and one sentence stating what causes a lunar eclipse, keeping them separate.
activities.insight: In ordinary phases Earth's shadow does not touch the Moon, so phases cannot be caused by it; Earth's shadow on the Moon is a separate, rare event (a lunar eclipse).

activities.title: Map position in orbit to shape in the sky (coupled dual view)
steps: Look at an overhead 'space view' showing the Moon at several positions around Earth, with its lit half always facing the Sun.
For a chosen orbit position, predict the shape you would see from Earth before checking the matching 'tonight's sky' Earth-view.

Drag or step the Moon around the orbit and watch the Earth-view shape change: full when the Moon is on the far side from the Sun, thinning to a crescent as it swings towards the Sun, vanishing at new moon.

Connect the repeating phases to the Moon’s motion around Earth: a full phase cycle is about a month. The orbital period relative to the stars is slightly shorter than the phase cycle because Earth is also moving around the Sun.
activities.insight: The Moon’s position relative to the Sun and Earth determines the phase seen from Earth. Both the orbital period and phase cycle are roughly a month, but they are not exactly the same period.

activities.title: Fly to Earth's surface and look up (spatial extension)
steps: Using a 3D model, orbit the camera to view the Sun-Earth-Moon system from space, keeping the Moon's lit hemisphere always facing the Sun.
Drop the camera down to stand on Earth's surface and look up at the Moon for the current orbit position.
Compare the shape you see looking up with the lit half shown in the space view, and explain why they match.
activities.insight: Standing on Earth and looking up connects the Moon's orbital position directly to the shape you would actually see in the sky.

activities.title: Reference diagram and recap of the 8 phases
steps: Study a labelled diagram of the eight phase positions around the orbit: new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.
Reveal or state the name and Earth-view shape for each position.
On the full-moon position, note that it is usually a full phase and only a lunar eclipse at the rare special alignment, keeping phase and eclipse distinct.
Order the phases into the correct cycle and say which way the lit part grows (waxing) and shrinks (waning).
activities.insight: The named phases form a repeating cycle around the orbit, and the full-moon position is normally just a phase, not an eclipse.

activities.title: Check and explain: two-tier phase questions
steps: Answer whether this statement is right: 'The crescent happens because Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon' — then explain WHY in your own words.
Choose what causes Moon phases from options that include the Earth's-shadow idea as a tempting wrong answer, and justify your choice.
Match each orbit position to the shape seen from Earth, and put the phases in order.

Answer the probes: where does the Moon's glow come from if it makes no light? At a thin crescent, is the rest of the Moon gone or just not lit towards us? How is a lunar eclipse different from a crescent? How long is one orbit and phase cycle?
activities.insight: Being able to reject the shadow explanation and give the reflected-light, viewing-angle reason shows understanding rather than only memorised phase names.

checkQuestion: Some people think the Moon's phases — like the thin crescent — happen because the EARTH'S shadow falls on the Moon and hides part of it. Is that right? If not, what really causes the phases? And does the Moon make its own light? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: No — Earth's shadow is not what causes the ordinary phases. The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight, so the half of the Moon facing the Sun is always lit. As the Moon orbits Earth (about once a month), we see different amounts of that lit half from where we stand — sometimes all of it (full), sometimes a sliver (crescent), sometimes none (new). That changing VIEW of the lit half, not Earth's shadow, makes the phases. (Earth's shadow does fall on the Moon occasionally — but that is a rare, separate event called a lunar eclipse.)
